ShellCheck's check-extra-masked-returns never flags a plain x=$(producer), never looks at a file redirection, exempts echo, dirname, basename, printf, set and shopt, and sees nothing when a producer exits 0 on a partial failure. This check parses each file with shfmt (shfmt -ln bash --to-json) and walks its typed tree under six rules, each a closed set; a finding is printed as file:line: <rule>: <message>: a. substitution: a command substitution ($(…) or backquotes) is accepted only as the whole value of the one assignment of a statement with no command word, where that statement is the last of an if or while condition (negated or not) or the left side of a || whose branch handles the status, and no statement on the path from the tested statement to the top level (the statement itself, the || list, and every block, subshell, list, if, loop or function body around it) runs in the background, is negated (the condition's own ! aside) or is a coproc, and no process substitution (<(…), >(…)) is on that path: ! x=$(…) || exit 1 reads the failure as success, x=$(…) || exit 1 &, { x=$(…) || exit 1; } & and ( x=$(…) || exit 1 ) & end only the background job, coproc { x=$(…); } || exit 1 tests the coprocess's start, cat <(x=$(…) || exit 1) and tee >(x=$(…) || exit 1) run the read in a child whose status the parent never sees (measured: bash goes on with exit 0), and each is a finding naming the flagged statement's or the substitution's line. A function body is not the top level: f() { x=$(…) || return 1; } is judged by its own path, whatever f & does at the call. The branches that handle the status are a closed list: (i) a plain command whose known first word is exit or return, as the whole branch, with no argument (the status of the failed substitution propagates), with one argument whose known text is a decimal from 1 to 255, or with one argument that is the bare $? (exit 0, exit "$x", exit $(cmd), exit 1 2 and return 0 are findings: a zero turns the failed read into success); (ii) a plain command whose known first word is one of REFUSAL_NAMES below (refuse, fail: the two refusal functions the adopted levers define, a closed allowlist; a denylist of bash builtins and reserved words cannot be complete, and fc was the one the tuple this lint carried missed, so fc() { exit 2; }; unset -f fc; x=$(false) || fc -l ran the builtin and the script went on) and names a function this file defines exactly once, at the top level, in the foreground and not negated, before the tested statement in file order, whose body is the refusal grammar: zero or more statements, each a plain command whose known first word is echo or printf with a redirect that sends fd 1 to fd 2 (>&2 or 1>&2), then exactly one last statement, a plain command exit with one argument whose known text is a decimal from 1 to 255, every statement in the foreground and not negated, and nothing else of any kind: no return, no $?, no local, no if, no assignment, no second exit, no call of another function, no command substitution anywhere in the body. Every definition of the name counts, at any depth: a second one inside an if, a loop, a block, a subshell or another function (refuse() { exit 2; }; if true; then refuse() { return 0; }; fi) or a second spelling (function refuse { …; }) is a finding naming both lines, since bash runs whichever ran last; a definition run in the background (fail() { exit 2; } &) exists in a child shell only; one after the tested statement has not run when the read fails; a call of any other defined name (die, true, fc, …) is a finding saying the name is not a refusal name, whatever its body; each is a finding naming the duplicate's line, the flag or the name. The body is matched, not analysed: f() { echo failed >&2; return $?; }, f() { return 0; exit 1; }, f() { echo x; exit 2; } and f() { local m=$1; echo "$m" >&2; exit 2; } are each a finding naming the function and the first statement outside the grammar, by line, whatever they would do when run (a name no function defines is a plain command; a function that cleans up before it exits is not a refusal function: the cleanup goes in a trap, or the call carries an allow comment naming the cleanup line); (iii) a block or subshell whose statements are that grammar ({ echo no >&2; exit 1; }), with return <1-255> as the one terminator instead when the branch is a brace block and the || list sits inside a function body of the file (a sourced helper returns where a lever exits: regime-env's || { echo … >&2; return 1; } blocks; a return at the top level of a script is a bash error, so it ends nothing there and stays a finding; U216b), never when the branch is a subshell, whose return ends the subshell alone while the function goes on (measured on bash 3.2: f() { x=$(false) || ( echo no >&2; return 1 ); echo on; }; if f; then echo ok; fi prints on and ok; U216c), so a bare exit or return, a return outside every function body or inside a subshell, a call of a refusal function or a $? inside one is a finding; (iv) a bare plain assignment (=, not +=) of exactly $? (status=$?; status+=$? adds the status to the value, 25 and 6 making 256, and is a finding naming the append). A branch statement run in the background (exit 2 &) or negated (! exit 1, ! (exit 1)) handles nothing. Any other branch leaves the substitution a finding that names the branch's shape: a pipeline, an && or || list, an if, a case, true, :, false or any other plain command, a block or subshell outside the grammar, an assignment of anything else, a first word with no known text. A later line that handles an empty value is not a branch: such a read carries # producer-status: allow <reason naming that line> (rule e). A word has a known text only when every part is a bare literal over the closed character set (letters, digits and _ - . / : = + @ % ,), a plain single-quoted string, or double quotes around literals (any character there) and such strings; * ? [ ] { } ~ $, a backquote, a backslash, whitespace or any other character in a bare literal, an expansion, an ANSI-C $'…' or a locale $"…" string make the word unknown, and nothing is decoded. Every other position is a finding at the line where the substitution opens: an argument, a local, export, declare or readonly, a redirect target, an unquoted heredoc body, [[ ]], an arithmetic expansion, a for list, a case word, a plain assignment whose status only set -e sees, two assignments in one statement, and a substitution inside another one. b. producer: a command whose leading words (known texts, as above) match a row of status-blind-producers.tsv beside this script (git ls-files, git config -f, git config --file, find, ls) must capture its stderr to a file, and a later statement of the same list must test [[ ! -s <that file> ]] in a shape whose failure stops the script: the last statement of an if condition, or the left side of a || whose branch is one of the forms of rule a, judged in the same function context as a tested read's branch (inside a function body a brace block ending in return <1-255> closes the producer, a subshell ending in return does not; U216c); a bare [[ ! -s <file> ]] statement is accepted only at the top level of a file whose prologue (rule c) runs set -euo pipefail before it, where set -e ends the script on its failure, and anywhere else (a function body, a block, a file with no prologue before it) is not a test. The producer statement, the test statement and every statement on the path of each to the top level must be in the foreground and not negated, with no process substitution on the path: git ls-files > l 2> e & lets the next statement test e before the listing has finished, ! git ls-files > l 2> e reads its failure as success, { git ls-files > l 2> e; } & ends only the job, coproc git ls-files > l 2> e tests the coprocess's start and done < <(git ls-files) runs it in a child whose failure the parent never sees, so each is a finding naming the flag and its line whatever follows it; ! [[ ! -s err ]] || exit 1 reads a non-empty file as clean, [[ ! -s err ]] & ends only the job, and an && list or a pipeline is not a test, so a producer whose only such statement is one of those is a finding naming that statement's line and why. Stderr is captured only when the last redirect of the statement that touches fd 2 is 2>, 2>> or 2>| to a word whose known text is not /dev/null, or whose parts are literals and parameter expansions (a process substitution, 2> >(tee e), is neither, and one among a producer's words, ls <(…), has no known text). The descriptor written before an operator is read as bash reads it, a decimal (02>&1 and 002> err name fd 2; one that is not all digits, {fd}>, refuses the file, exit 2). A redirect touches fd 2 when that descriptor is 2 whatever the operator, when it is &> or &>>, or when it is >& or <& to a word that is not a plain descriptor (all digits or -), whatever the descriptor before it: >&file and 1>&file send both streams to the file, >&2-, 1>&2- and <&2- move fd 2 and close it, >&$fd may be any of them when it runs; >&2, 1>&2, 01>&2 and >&- leave fd 2 alone. Any other operator there (2>&N, 2<&-, 2<, 2<>, 2<<<, &>, >&file, a move, one shfmt adds later) leaves stderr uncaptured, and the word of a >& or <& is never the captured file. The tested word names the same file only when both texts are known and equal, or both hold a parameter expansion and their parts are equal. read_listing of scripts/orchestrator/read-lib.sh is that shape by construction, and a producer the table does not name is not held to this rule. c. prologue: the file runs set -euo pipefail at top level, in the foreground and not negated, before its first statement holding a command substitution (a function body counts), else a finding at line 1 naming why the first set -euo pipefail the file holds does not count: set -euo pipefail &, { set -euo pipefail; } & and ( set -euo pipefail ) set the options of a child shell only, one inside a function, block or if is not at the top level. shopt -s inherit_errexit is not required: bash 3.2 has no such option. d. read: a read that carries its own < redirect is a finding naming read_file (done < file redirects the loop, not the read; a here-string is not a file). e. allow: # producer-status: allow <reason> on the statement's first line exempts that statement from a, b and d; an allow comment with no reason is itself a finding and exempts nothing. The enforced file set is tests/unit/test_producer_status_check.py (the library and the five levers), not a Makefile target. f. shadow and binding: the rules above trust a closed set of names by their spelling, GUARDED_NAMES below, one dict with a reason per name: the builtins the rules read (set, c; exit, return, a form i; echo, printf, the refusal grammar; read, d), the refusal functions (refuse, fail, a form ii), the rebinders of this rule (REBINDERS, so the set is closed over itself: alias command=eval had passed, and command 'refuse() { return 0; }' then redefined the refusal function through a word this rule read as its own), the library's arrays (GIT_ISOLATED_ENV, exported word by word before every git; GIT_ISOLATED_ARGS, GIT_ISOLATED_SCRUB_NAMES), the directory the one accepted source reads from (LEVER_DIR), the variables that bind a command word (PATH, BASH_ALIASES, BASH_CMDS) and the ones bash itself reads when it runs a lever (BASH_ENV, ENV, SHELLOPTS, BASHOPTS, IFS, CDPATH, BASH_LOADABLES_PATH, EXECIGNORE, PS4). tests/unit/test_producer_status_check.py holds every literal name this walk compares against to that set, so it cannot drift; the producers' first words come from the table and are protected as command words only. shadow, the command words: a function definition of any name the rules read as a command word (interpreted: the builtins, the producers, the refusal names, the rebinders), at any depth and in any spelling (set() { :; } lets a warned listing pass a bare [[ ! -s err ]], since the set -euo pipefail the test relies on ran a function; exit() { :; }, git() { command git "$@"; return 0; }, eval() { :; }), is a finding at its definition line naming what it shadows (a refusal name's definitions are judged by form ii: one, at top level, before the read). So is every other way bash offers to rebind a word or to run text this walk has not read, a plain command whose known first word is one of REBINDERS, read as bash reads that word (SKIPS_OPTIONS: for a NAMER, a FORWARDER, trap, mapfile and readarray the leading - words are options read for their letters, -- ends them, a letter with an argument takes it, hash -p /x, and a + word is an argument; source, . and eval skip nothing, every argument word is the file or the text; a call left with no argument to judge, source, enable -n, hash -p /usr/bin/true, is a finding, hash -r, whose option is the whole job, aside): an ALIASER (alias, unalias) in any form, alias -p and alias ll='ls -l' included, since no lever defines an alias and non-interactive bash expands none unless shopt -s expand_aliases is set, so the rule has no alias to accept (measured: the auditor's bypass exits 127 without that option and runs on with exit 0 under it); the EXPANDER (shopt) with expand_aliases among its arguments in any spelling (-s, -qs, -u, after --) or with an argument that has no known text (shopt -s inherit_errexit and shopt -q nullglob pass); a NAMER (enable, hash, unset) with an argument whose known text, before any =, is such a name (enable -n echo, enable -n command, hash -p /x/true refuse, unset -f refuse, and unset refuse, which removes the function when no variable has the name) or with an argument that has no known text (unset "$name"; unset -v names variables only and binds nothing, INERT_OPTIONS); a FORWARDER (builtin, command) whose arguments name such a word or have no known text (command git ls-files runs past rule b), and whose command is judged again when its own first word is a rebinder (command unset -f refuse, command alias x=y; command -v and -V print and run nothing); a RUNNER whose text or file this walk has not read: eval with any argument, source and . with any argument but the one accepted shape, . "${LEVER_DIR}/git-isolated.sh", . "${LEVER_DIR}/read-lib.sh" or . "${LEVER_DIR}/regime-env", the three libraries the levers source (LIBRARY_DIR, LIBRARY_FILES; the parts of the one argument, nothing else), trap with an action that is not empty, - or one simple command whose first word is no rebinder (trap cleanup EXIT and trap 'rm -f "${f}"' EXIT are read whole; trap 'refuse() { :; }' DEBUG redefines the function before the next command runs), mapfile or readarray with -C (the callback is text bash runs). binding, the writes: a write to a guarded name is (a) an Assign node whose name is guarded, with or without a value, wherever it sits (a plain assignment, a command's prefix, IFS= read -r x, a declaration's argument, export PATH=/x/bin, declare -a GIT_ISOLATED_ENV=(x); shfmt writes no Value for PATH=, which writes the empty string, nor for the bare name of export PATH or declare +x -a GIT_ISOLATED_ENV, each a write too); (b) the variable of a for or select, and an expansion that assigns its parameter (${PATH=x}, ${PATH:=x}); (c) a word in any position (an argument of any command, a prefix's value, an array element, a for list, a case pattern, a test or arithmetic operand, a redirect target, a coprocess name, a heredoc body bash expands) whose leading literal parts spell an assignment to a guarded name (WRITES: export 'PATH=/x/bin:$PATH', env PATH=/x/bin git ls-files, 'GIT_ISOLATED_ENV=PATH=/x/bin', alias fail=true) or its literal parts hold the name of a guarded variable as a token (every guarded name the shadow part does not read as a command word: read -r PATH, printf -v PATH x, unset PATH, mapfile PATH, local -n ref=PATH, (( PATH = 1 )), ${a[PATH=1]}, let 'PATH = 1', unset 'a[PATH=1]', bash -c 'cd /; PATH=x git', a message that names it); a bare literal, a single-quoted, double-quoted, ANSI-C or locale string is a literal part, the name is matched in the concatenation of every literal part, quotes removed and in order (printf -v PA"TH" x, PA'TH'=1, 'PA'TH=1; measured: each sets PATH), and in each part alone, and an expansion among them contributes no text and hides none; (d) a word of a declaration (declare, typeset, readonly, export, local, directly or through builtin or command) with no known text, which may spell any write (export "$binding", export "${GIT_ISOLATED_ENV[@]}"; a forwarder's own unknown argument is the shadow finding above as well); (e) a declaration option under which a later assignment writes elsewhere (declare -i, local -n; ATTRIBUTE_OPTIONS); (f) an operand where bash evaluates arithmetic ((( )), $(( )), let, a C-style for, an array index or a slice, an operand of -eq, -ne, -lt, -le, -gt, -ge, of -v or -R) that is not digits, operators and whitespace alone (ARITHMETIC_INERT): bash evaluates a name there recursively (measured on bash 3.2: y='PATH=1' then (( y, 1 )), (( $y, 1 )), [[ y -eq 1 ]], a[y]=1, let 'y + 1' and declare -i x; x=$y each set PATH), so a name, a $, an expansion or a substitution there is a write to any guarded name unless the exact text of its statement, in its file, is a row of ACCEPTED_ARITHMETIC (the statements of the adopted set, measured and listed there: the $# tests, the status and counter comparisons and increments, exit $((128 + $2)), the fetch retry for; $#, $? and ${#name} are rows too, no reading of which parameters are numbers is kept). The walk visits every node of every statement and asks those questions of each; there is no list of positions. A write is accepted only when the exact text of its statement, in its file, is a row of ACCEPTED_WRITES, the writes the adopted set makes (measured and listed there: the IFS= prefixes of the levers' read lines, LEVER_DIR=${dir} of every self-check, the library's three arrays, their declare, the unset loop over their names, export "${GIT_ISOLATED_ENV[@]}", the messages that name a guarded variable); any other is a finding naming the name, how it is written, the statement's kind and the line. Not read: an expansion handed to an external command (env "$x" git, sudo "$x": that command's argument, which the shell does not bind; the one the library hands env is the array a row pins), a name an expansion carries into a builtin that is no declaration (unset -v "$name" of the scrubs, printf -v "$3" of the readers, read -r "$name": the caller's name, by design), and a literal heredoc body (data, skipped by every scan). An allow comment exempts nothing in rule f. A heredoc body whose delimiter has any quoted or escaped part is literal and skipped, as bash reads it (shfmt expands the body of a partly quoted delimiter such as <<'E'OF), by every scan of this walk: one function, children, is the only descent into a node, so a $(refuse() { return 0; }) or a # producer-status: allow in such a body defines and exempts nothing. The files are parsed as bash. A file shfmt cannot parse is refused, never read as clean. Before any listed file is read, scripts/ci/shfmt_json_contract.py proves that the pinned shfmt still produces the node kinds and fields this walk reads, and this walk then visits the contract fixtures itself and is refused if it sees no statement, no assignment or no command substitution there (regime-cutover U105): "no findings" on the listed files is never "saw nothing".

#   printed as `file:line: <rule>: <message>`:

#      grammar, by line, whatever they would do when run (a name no function defines is a plain command; a function that
#      cleans up before it exits is not a refusal function: the cleanup goes in a trap, or the call carries an allow
#      comment naming the cleanup line); (iii) a block or subshell whose statements are that grammar (`{ echo no >&2;
#      exit 1; }`), with `return <1-255>` as the one terminator instead when the branch is a brace block and the `||`
#      list sits inside a function body of the file (a sourced helper returns where a lever exits: regime-env's `|| {
#      echo … >&2; return 1; }` blocks; a `return` at the top level of a script is a bash error, so it ends nothing
#      there and stays a finding; U216b), never when the branch is a subshell, whose `return` ends the subshell alone
#      while the function goes on (measured on bash 3.2: `f() { x=$(false) || ( echo no >&2; return 1 ); echo on; };
#      if f; then echo ok; fi` prints `on` and `ok`; U216c), so a bare `exit` or `return`, a `return` outside every
#      function body or inside a subshell, a call of a refusal function or a `$?` inside one is a finding; (iv) a
#      bare plain assignment (`=`, not `+=`) of exactly `$?` (`status=$?`;
#      `status+=$?` adds the status to the value, 25
#      and 6 making 256, and is a finding naming the append). A branch statement run in the background (`exit 2 &`) or
#      negated (`! exit 1`, `! (exit 1)`) handles nothing.
#      Any other branch leaves the substitution a finding that names the branch's shape: a pipeline, an `&&` or `||`
#      list, an `if`, a `case`, `true`, `:`, `false` or any other plain command, a block or subshell outside the
#      grammar, an assignment of anything else, a first word with no known text. A later line that handles an
#      empty value is not a branch: such a read carries `# producer-status: allow <reason naming that line>` (rule
#      e). A word has a known text only when every part is a bare literal over the closed character set (letters,
#      digits and `_ - . / : = + @ % ,`), a plain single-quoted string, or double quotes around literals (any
#      character there) and such strings; `* ? [ ] { } ~ $`, a backquote, a backslash, whitespace or any other
#      character in a bare literal, an expansion, an ANSI-C `$'…'` or a locale `$"…"` string make the word unknown,
#      and nothing is decoded. Every other position is a finding at the line where the substitution opens: an
#      argument, a `local`, `export`, `declare` or `readonly`, a redirect target, an unquoted heredoc body, `[[ ]]`,
#      an arithmetic expansion, a `for` list, a `case` word, a plain assignment whose status only `set -e` sees, two
#      assignments in one statement, and a substitution inside another one.
#   b. `producer`: a command whose leading words (known texts, as above) match a row of status-blind-producers.tsv
#      beside this script (`git ls-files`, `git config -f`, `git config --file`, `find`, `ls`) must capture its
#      stderr to a file, and a later statement of the same list must test `[[ ! -s <that file> ]]` in a shape whose
#      failure stops the script: the last statement of an `if` condition, or the left side of a `||` whose branch is
#      one of the forms of rule a, judged in the same function context as a tested read's branch (inside a function
#      body a brace block ending in `return <1-255>` closes the producer, a subshell ending in `return` does not;
#      U216c); a bare `[[ ! -s <file> ]]` statement is accepted only at the top level of a file whose prologue (rule
#      c) runs `set -euo pipefail` before it, where `set -e` ends the script on its failure, and anywhere else (a
#      function body, a block, a file with no prologue before it) is not a test. The producer
#      statement, the test statement and every statement on the path of each to the top level must be in the
#      foreground and not negated, with no process substitution on the path: `git ls-files > l 2> e &` lets the next
#      statement test `e` before the listing has finished, `! git ls-files > l 2> e` reads its failure as success, `{
#      git ls-files > l 2> e; } &` ends only the job, `coproc git ls-files > l 2> e` tests the coprocess's start and
#      `done < <(git ls-files)` runs it in a child whose failure the parent never sees, so each is a finding naming
#      the flag and its line whatever follows it; `! [[ ! -s err ]] || exit 1` reads a non-empty file as clean, `[[ !
#      -s err ]] &` ends only the job, and an `&&` list or a pipeline is not a test, so a producer whose only such
#      statement is one of those is a finding naming that statement's line and why. Stderr is captured only when the
#      last redirect of the statement that touches fd 2 is `2>`, `2>>` or `2>|` to a word whose known text is not
#      /dev/null, or whose parts are literals and parameter expansions (a process substitution, `2> >(tee e)`, is
#      neither, and one among a producer's words, `ls <(…)`, has no known text). The descriptor written before an
#      operator is read as bash reads it, a decimal (`02>&1` and `002> err` name fd 2; one that is not all digits,
#      `{fd}>`, refuses the file, exit 2). A redirect touches fd 2 when that descriptor is 2 whatever the operator,
#      when it is `&>` or `&>>`, or when it is `>&` or `<&` to a word that is not a plain descriptor (all digits or
#      `-`), whatever the descriptor before it: `>&file` and `1>&file` send both streams to the file, `>&2-`, `1>&2-`
#      and `<&2-` move fd 2 and close it, `>&$fd` may be any of them when it runs; `>&2`, `1>&2`, `01>&2` and `>&-`
#      leave fd 2 alone. Any other operator there (`2>&N`, `2<&-`, `2<`, `2<>`, `2<<<`, `&>`, `>&file`, a move, one
#      shfmt adds later) leaves stderr uncaptured, and the word of a `>&` or `<&` is never the captured file. The
#      tested word names the same file only when both texts are known and
#      equal, or both hold a parameter expansion and their parts are equal. `read_listing` of
#      scripts/orchestrator/read-lib.sh is that shape by construction, and a producer the table does not name is not
#      held to this rule.
#   c. `prologue`: the file runs `set -euo pipefail` at top level, in the foreground and not negated, before its
#      first statement holding a command substitution (a function body counts), else a finding at line 1 naming why
#      the first `set -euo pipefail` the file holds does not count: `set -euo pipefail &`, `{ set -euo pipefail; } &`
#      and `( set -euo pipefail )` set the options of a child shell only, one inside a function, block or `if` is
#      not at the top level. `shopt -s inherit_errexit` is not required: bash 3.2 has no such option.
#   d. `read`: a `read` that carries its own `<` redirect is a finding naming `read_file` (`done < file` redirects
#      the loop, not the `read`; a here-string is not a file).
#   e. `allow`: `# producer-status: allow <reason>` on the statement's first line exempts that statement from a, b
#      and d; an allow comment with no reason is itself a finding and exempts nothing. The enforced file set is
#      tests/unit/test_producer_status_check.py (the library and the five levers), not a Makefile target.
#   f. `shadow` and `binding`: the rules above trust a closed set of names by their spelling, GUARDED_NAMES below, one
#      dict with a reason per name: the builtins the rules read (`set`, c; `exit`, `return`, a form i; `echo`,
#      `printf`, the refusal grammar; `read`, d), the refusal functions (`refuse`, `fail`, a form ii), the rebinders of
#      this rule (REBINDERS, so the set is closed over itself: `alias command=eval` had passed, and `command 'refuse()
#      { return 0; }'` then redefined the refusal function through a word this rule read as its own), the library's
#      arrays (`GIT_ISOLATED_ENV`, exported word by word before every git; `GIT_ISOLATED_ARGS`,
#      `GIT_ISOLATED_SCRUB_NAMES`), the directory the one accepted `source` reads from (`LEVER_DIR`), the variables
#      that bind a command word (`PATH`, `BASH_ALIASES`, `BASH_CMDS`) and the ones bash itself reads when it runs a
#      lever (`BASH_ENV`, `ENV`, `SHELLOPTS`, `BASHOPTS`, `IFS`, `CDPATH`, `BASH_LOADABLES_PATH`, `EXECIGNORE`, `PS4`).
#      tests/unit/test_producer_status_check.py holds every literal name this walk compares against to that set, so
#      it cannot drift; the producers' first words come from the table and are protected as command words only.
#      `shadow`, the command words: a function definition of any name the rules read as a command word (interpreted:
#      the builtins, the producers, the refusal names, the rebinders), at any depth and in any spelling (`set() { :;
#      }` lets a warned listing pass a bare `[[ ! -s err ]]`, since the `set -euo pipefail` the test relies on ran a
#      function; `exit() { :; }`, `git() { command git "$@"; return 0; }`, `eval() { :; }`), is a finding at its
#      definition line naming what it shadows (a refusal name's definitions are judged by form ii: one, at top level,
#      before the read). So is every other way bash offers to rebind a word or to run text this walk has not read, a
#      plain command whose known first word is one of REBINDERS, read as bash reads that word (SKIPS_OPTIONS: for a
#      NAMER, a FORWARDER, `trap`, `mapfile` and `readarray` the leading `-` words are options read for their letters,
#      `--` ends them, a letter with an argument takes it, `hash -p /x`, and a `+` word is an argument; `source`, `.`
#      and `eval` skip nothing, every argument word is the file or the text; a call left with no argument to judge,
#      `source`, `enable -n`, `hash -p /usr/bin/true`, is a finding, `hash -r`, whose option is the whole job, aside):
#      an ALIASER (`alias`, `unalias`) in any form, `alias -p` and `alias ll='ls -l'` included, since no lever defines
#      an alias and non-interactive bash expands none unless `shopt -s expand_aliases` is set, so the rule has no
#      alias to accept (measured: the auditor's bypass exits 127 without that option and runs on with exit 0 under
#      it); the EXPANDER (`shopt`) with `expand_aliases` among its arguments in any spelling (`-s`, `-qs`, `-u`, after
#      `--`) or with an argument that has no known text (`shopt -s inherit_errexit` and `shopt -q nullglob` pass); a
#      NAMER (`enable`, `hash`, `unset`) with an argument whose known text, before any `=`, is such a name (`enable -n
#      echo`, `enable -n command`, `hash -p /x/true refuse`, `unset -f refuse`, and `unset refuse`, which removes the
#      function when no variable has the name) or with an argument that has no known text (`unset "$name"`; `unset
#      -v` names variables only and binds nothing, INERT_OPTIONS); a FORWARDER (`builtin`, `command`) whose arguments
#      name such a word or have no known text (`command git ls-files` runs past rule b), and whose command is judged
#      again when its own first word is a rebinder (`command unset -f refuse`, `command alias x=y`; `command -v` and
#      `-V` print and run nothing); a RUNNER whose text or file this walk has not read: `eval` with any argument,
#      `source` and `.` with any argument but the one accepted shape, `. "${LEVER_DIR}/git-isolated.sh"`, `.
#      "${LEVER_DIR}/read-lib.sh"` or `. "${LEVER_DIR}/regime-env"`, the three libraries the levers source
#      (LIBRARY_DIR, LIBRARY_FILES; the parts of the one argument, nothing else), `trap` with an action that is not
#      empty, `-` or one simple command whose
#      first word is no rebinder (`trap cleanup EXIT` and `trap 'rm -f "${f}"' EXIT` are read whole; `trap 'refuse()
#      { :; }' DEBUG` redefines the function before the next command runs), `mapfile` or `readarray` with `-C` (the
#      callback is text bash runs).
#      `binding`, the writes: a write to a guarded name is (a) an Assign node whose name is guarded, with or without
#      a value, wherever it sits (a plain assignment, a command's prefix, `IFS= read -r x`, a declaration's argument,
#      `export PATH=/x/bin`, `declare -a GIT_ISOLATED_ENV=(x)`; shfmt writes no Value for `PATH=`, which writes the
#      empty string, nor for the bare name of `export PATH` or `declare +x -a GIT_ISOLATED_ENV`, each a write too);
#      (b) the variable of a `for` or `select`, and an expansion that assigns its parameter (`${PATH=x}`,
#      `${PATH:=x}`); (c) a word in any position (an argument of any command, a prefix's value, an array element, a
#      `for` list, a `case` pattern, a test or arithmetic operand, a redirect target, a coprocess name, a heredoc body
#      bash expands) whose leading literal parts spell an assignment to a guarded name (WRITES: `export
#      'PATH=/x/bin:$PATH'`, `env PATH=/x/bin git ls-files`, `'GIT_ISOLATED_ENV=PATH=/x/bin'`, `alias fail=true`) or
#      its literal parts hold the name of a guarded variable as a token (every guarded name the shadow part does not
#      read as a command word: `read -r PATH`, `printf -v PATH x`, `unset PATH`, `mapfile PATH`, `local -n ref=PATH`,
#      `(( PATH = 1 ))`, `${a[PATH=1]}`, `let 'PATH = 1'`, `unset 'a[PATH=1]'`, `bash -c 'cd /; PATH=x git'`, a
#      message that names it); a bare literal, a single-quoted, double-quoted, ANSI-C or locale string is a literal
#      part, the name is matched in the concatenation of every literal part, quotes removed and in order (`printf -v
#      PA"TH" x`, `PA'TH'=1`, `'PA'TH=1`; measured: each sets PATH), and in each part alone, and an expansion among
#      them contributes no text and hides none; (d) a word of a declaration (`declare`, `typeset`, `readonly`,
#      `export`, `local`, directly or through `builtin` or `command`) with no known text, which may spell any write
#      (`export "$binding"`, `export "${GIT_ISOLATED_ENV[@]}"`; a forwarder's own unknown argument is the shadow
#      finding above as well); (e) a declaration option under which a later assignment writes elsewhere (`declare
#      -i`, `local -n`; ATTRIBUTE_OPTIONS); (f) an operand where bash evaluates arithmetic (`(( ))`, `$(( ))`, `let`,
#      a C-style `for`, an array index or a slice, an operand of `-eq`, `-ne`, `-lt`, `-le`, `-gt`, `-ge`, of `-v` or
#      `-R`) that is not digits, operators and whitespace alone (ARITHMETIC_INERT): bash evaluates a name there
#      recursively (measured on bash 3.2: `y='PATH=1'` then `(( y, 1 ))`, `(( $y, 1 ))`, `[[ y -eq 1 ]]`, `a[y]=1`,
#      `let 'y + 1'` and `declare -i x; x=$y` each set PATH), so a name, a `$`, an expansion or a substitution there is
#      a write to any guarded name unless the exact text of its statement, in its file, is a row of
#      ACCEPTED_ARITHMETIC (the statements of the adopted set, measured and listed there: the `$#` tests, the status
#      and counter comparisons and increments, `exit $((128 + $2))`, the fetch retry `for`; `$#`, `$?` and `${#name}`
#      are rows too, no reading of which parameters are numbers is kept). The walk visits every node of every
#      statement and asks those questions of each; there is no list of positions. A write is accepted only when the
#      exact text of its statement, in its file, is a row of ACCEPTED_WRITES, the writes the adopted set makes
#      (measured and listed there: the `IFS=` prefixes of the levers' `read` lines, `LEVER_DIR=${dir}` of every
#      self-check, the library's three arrays, their `declare`, the `unset` loop over their names, `export
#      "${GIT_ISOLATED_ENV[@]}"`, the messages that name a guarded variable); any other is a finding naming the name,
#      how it is written, the statement's kind and the line. Not read: an expansion handed to an external command
#      (`env "$x" git`, `sudo "$x"`: that command's argument, which the shell does not bind; the one the library hands
#      `env` is the array a row pins), a name an expansion carries into a builtin that is no declaration (`unset -v
#      "$name"` of the scrubs, `printf -v "$3"` of the readers, `read -r "$name"`: the caller's name, by design), and a
#      literal heredoc body (data, skipped by every scan). An allow comment exempts nothing in rule f.
#   A heredoc body whose delimiter has any quoted or escaped part is literal and skipped, as bash reads it (shfmt
#   expands the body of a partly quoted delimiter such as `<<'E'OF`), by every scan of this walk: one function,
#   children, is the only descent into a node, so a `$(refuse() { return 0; })` or a `# producer-status: allow` in
#   such a body defines and exempts nothing. The files are parsed as bash. A file shfmt
#   cannot parse is refused, never read as clean. Before any listed file is read, scripts/ci/shfmt_json_contract.py
#   proves that the pinned shfmt still produces the node kinds and fields this walk reads, and this walk then visits
#   the contract fixtures itself and is refused if it sees no statement, no assignment or no command substitution
#   there (regime-cutover U105): "no findings" on the listed files is never "saw nothing".
# @arg $@ path The files to check.
# @description The shfmt is PATH's, the one scripts/ci/pinned-tool-version.sh checks ([tools."http:shfmt"], U97);
#   no variable selects another, and no variable selects another producer table.
# @exitcode 0 No finding.
# @exitcode 1 At least one finding, each printed as `file:line: <rule>: <message>`.
# @exitcode 2 No file given, a listed file cannot be read or parsed, shfmt or python3 is missing, shfmt's JSON does
#   not match the pinned node table, the producer table is missing or malformed, a listed file holds no statement
#   (empty or comment-only) or a redirect descriptor that is not a decimal (`{fd}>`), or this walk saw none of a
#   listed file's statements or none of its kinds in the contract fixtures: the list is refused, never read as clean.
# @example
#   scripts/ci/producer-status-check.sh scripts/orchestrator/read-lib.sh scripts/orchestrator/records-sync.sh
set -euo pipefail

if (($# == 0)); then
    echo "producer-status-check: no file to check; an empty list is refused" >&2
    exit 2
fi

for tool in shfmt python3; do
    if ! command -v "${tool}" > /dev/null; then
        echo "producer-status-check: ${tool} not found; the list is refused" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done

for file in "$@"; do
    if [[ ! -f ${file} || ! -r ${file} ]]; then
        echo "producer-status-check: cannot read ${file}; the list is refused" >&2
        exit 2
    fi
done

# The directory of this script, where scripts/ci/shfmt_json_contract.py and the producer table live: a parameter
# expansion, so no producer's status is at stake.
case ${BASH_SOURCE[0]} in
*/*) here=${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*} ;;
*) here=. ;;
esac
table=${here}/status-blind-producers.tsv
if [[ ! -f ${table} || ! -r ${table} ]]; then
    echo "producer-status-check: cannot read the producer table ${table}; the list is refused" >&2
    exit 2
fi

# Runs the contract, reads the producer table, then parses each file with shfmt and walks its typed JSON. argv[1]
# is the directory of shfmt_json_contract.py, argv[2] the producer table, the rest are the files. Exits 1 when it
# prints a finding, 2 when the list is refused.
walk=$(
    cat << 'PY'

import re
import subprocess
import sys
from collections import Counter

sys.path.insert(0, sys.argv[1])
import shfmt_json_contract as contract  # noqa: E402

NAME = "producer-status-check"
TABLE = sys.argv[2]
SUBSTITUTION, PRODUCER, PROLOGUE, READ, ALLOW = "substitution", "producer", "prologue", "read", "allow"
SHADOW = "shadow"  # rule f, a command word rebound

    READ: "`read` from a file takes a failed read for the end of the file; use read_file of read-lib.sh",
    ALLOW: "`# producer-status: allow` needs a reason after it",

# The names form (ii) accepts, a closed allowlist: the two refusal functions the adopted levers define. A denylist of
# bash builtins and reserved words cannot be complete (bash adds and loads them); the one this lint carried missed
# `fc`, so `fc() { exit 2; }; unset -f fc; x=$(false) || fc -l` ran the builtin and the script went on.
REFUSAL_NAMES = ("refuse", "fail")

# or whitespace is expanded or read by bash and is not decoded here. Inside double quotes bash expands none of them,
# so the set does not apply there.
KNOWN_CHARACTERS = frozenset("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789_-./:=+@%,")
# The last status as a whole word, `$?` or `${?}` (form iv); `${?:-0}` and `"$?"` are not it.
STATUS_PARAMETERS = (
    {"Type": "ParamExp", "Short": True, "Param": {"Value": "?"}},
    {"Type": "ParamExp", "Param": {"Value": "?"}},
)

# read's own statement and every statement around it (a `||` list, a block, a subshell, an `if`, a loop, a function
# body), and every process substitution around it (`<(…)`, `>(…)`: a child whose status the parent never sees, so
# the substitution itself is the flag; measured: `cat <(x=$(false) || exit 1); echo ran` prints `ran` and exits 0);
# a statement is flagged when it runs in the background (`&`), is negated (`!`) or runs a `coproc` clause.
BACKGROUND, NEGATED, COPROCESS, PROCESS = "Background", "Negated", "CoprocClause", "ProcSubst"
BRANCH_FLAGS = {  # how a finding names a flagged statement in a `||` branch
    BACKGROUND: "a command run in the background (`&`), which lets the script go on",
    NEGATED: "a negated command (`!`), whose failure status is read as success",
    COPROCESS: "a `coproc`, whose status is its start, not its command's",
    PROCESS: "a process substitution (`<(…)`, `>(…)`), whose failure the parent never sees",
}
DEFINITION_FLAGS = {  # how a finding names the flagged top-level definition of the function a `||` branch calls
    BACKGROUND: "runs in the background (`&`), so the function exists in a child shell only",
    NEGATED: "is negated (`!`), a flagged statement",
    COPROCESS: "runs in a coprocess, a child shell",
    PROCESS: "runs in a process substitution, a child shell",
}
WRITERS = ("echo", "printf")  # the plain commands a refusal body may run before its `exit`, each sending fd 1 to fd 2
STDOUT = 1  # the descriptor `1>&2` writes, as a number; `>&2` writes none
GRAMMAR = (  # how a finding names the refusal grammar (forms ii, iii); the second terminator is form iii's inside a function
    "`echo`/`printf` to stderr, then one `exit <1-255>`, or `return <1-255>` when the branch is a block inside a "
    "function body"
)
SHAPES = {  # how a finding names the command kind of a branch; a kind not listed is named by shfmt's type
    "Block": "a block",
    "Subshell": "a subshell",
    "IfClause": "an `if`",
    "CaseClause": "a `case`",
    "WhileClause": "a `while`",
    "ForClause": "a `for`",
    "DeclClause": "a declaration",
    "FuncDecl": "a function definition",
    "TestClause": "a `[[ ]]` test",
    "ArithmCmd": "an arithmetic command",
    "LetClause": "a `let`",
    "TimeClause": "a `time`",
    "CoprocClause": "a `coproc`",

LIST_SHAPES = {"|": "a pipeline", "&&": "an `&&` list", "||": "a `||` list"}
PROLOGUE_WORDS = ["set", "-euo", "pipefail"]
READER = "read"  # the builtin rule d holds away from a file; a function of that name shadows it
STDERR = 2  # a descriptor is read as a decimal, so `02>` and `002>` name it too
FILE_OPS = (">", ">>", ">|")  # the only operators that, on fd 2, capture stderr to the word's file
BOTH_OPS = ("&>", "&>>")  # touch fd 2 with no descriptor written

# Rule f's rebinders: every plain command bash offers that binds a command word to other text, a file, a builtin or
# nothing, or runs text this walk has not read, each read as bash reads it (measured on /bin/bash 3.2.57; the bash 4
# builtins by the manual). An ALIASER defines, prints or removes an alias (`alias`, `unalias`): no lever defines one,
# and non-interactive bash expands none unless `shopt -s expand_aliases` is set (or BASHOPTS is inherited), so every
# call is a finding, in any form, and so is the EXPANDER (`shopt`) naming EXPAND_ALIASES (measured: `alias

# -n command`, `hash -p /usr/bin/true command`, `unset -f eval` or `eval() { :; }` is a finding like `enable -n echo`.
